DOCUMENT:
Market Analysis: Launching a Digital Subscription for the Calderbrook Courier
Commercial Strategy, Calderbrook Media, April 2026

1. Purpose
The Calderbrook Courier's website is free to read and funded by display advertising, which has declined by about 12% a year for three years. This paper assesses the market for a metered digital subscription, in which readers can view five articles a month free before being asked to subscribe, and recommends a price and launch plan.

2. Our audience
The website had an average of 420,000 monthly unique users (MUU) in 2025, of whom around 60% live in the Courier's circulation area. The printed Courier has 11,200 subscribers paying £18.50 a month for six-day home delivery, plus around 6,000 daily news-stand sales. Print subscribers are older on average than web readers, and most also use the website.

In our March 2026 survey of print subscribers (1,850 responses), 30% said they would cancel their print subscription and take a digital-only subscription instead if one were offered at under £6 a month.

3. Evidence from comparable titles
We obtained data, under confidentiality agreements, from four regional titles that launched metered subscriptions between 2022 and 2024.

Table 1. Comparable regional titles, second year after launch
Title | Monthly unique users | Digital subscribers | Subscribers as % of MUU | Monthly price
Title A | 360,000 | 6,800 | 1.9% | £5.99
Title B | 280,000 | 3,100 | 1.1% | £4.99
Title C | 390,000 | 9,400 | 2.4% | £7.99
Title D | 300,000 | 4,200 | 1.4% | £3.99

All four titles reported that subscriber numbers stabilised by the end of the second year, and that churn settled at between 3% and 5% a month after promotional periods ended.

4. Price
Conversion rates across the comparable titles are highest for the titles charging the lowest prices, which suggests that our audience will respond best to a low price point. We therefore propose a price of £4.99 a month, with an introductory offer of £1 for the first three months.

5. Projection
The average conversion rate of the four comparable titles is 2.0% of MUU. Applied to our 420,000 MUU, that gives about 8,400 subscribers by the end of year two. At £4.99 a month, 8,400 subscribers would generate around £503,000 a year in subscription revenue.

Table 2. Year-two projection
Item | Annual amount
Subscription revenue | £503,000
Subscription platform and payment fees | £85,000
Marketing | £60,000
Net contribution | £358,000

We expect a modest reduction in display advertising revenue as page views from non-subscribers fall when they reach the meter; the comparable titles reported falls of 5% to 8% in page views. Our display revenue was £1.1 million in 2025, so a fall of this size would cost between £55,000 and £88,000 a year, which is well covered by the projected net contribution.

6. Launch plan
- Platform selection and integration: May to July 2026.
- Soft launch with a ten-article meter: September 2026.
- Full launch with a five-article meter: November 2026.
- Review of price and meter after six months.

7. Conclusion
The evidence from comparable titles shows a viable market for a Courier digital subscription. At £4.99 a month, a price that the comparable titles' experience suggests will maximise take-up, we project around 8,400 subscribers and a net contribution of £358,000 a year, more than offsetting the expected effect on display advertising. We recommend approval to proceed with the launch plan.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "The average conversion rate of the four comparable titles is 2.0% of MUU." -- (1.9 + 1.1 + 2.4 + 1.4) / 4 = 1.7%, not 2.0%. At 1.7% the projection is about 7,140 subscribers, not 8,400, and revenue about £428,000.
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Conversion rates across the comparable titles are highest for the titles charging the lowest prices" -- Table 1 shows the opposite pattern: the highest-priced title (C, £7.99) has the highest conversion (2.4%) and the lowest-priced (D, £3.99) has 1.4%. The pricing rationale rests on misreading the table.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "At £4.99 a month, 8,400 subscribers would generate around £503,000 a year in subscription revenue." -- The projection treats all subscription revenue as incremental, but the document's own survey says 30% of the 11,200 print subscribers (about 3,360) would cancel £18.50 print subscriptions for a digital one under £6. Switching would cost about £13.51 a month each (roughly £545,000 a year), which is never addressed although it could wipe out the net contribution.

REVIEW:
# Review: Calderbrook Courier Digital Subscription Market Analysis

The paper is clearly written, but its recommendation does not follow from its evidence. The pricing argument contradicts its own data. The headline conversion rate is miscalculated. It also leaves out print cannibalisation, which on the paper's own survey figures could exceed the projected net contribution.

## Major issues

### 1. The price argument contradicts Table 1

Section 4 says conversion is "highest for the titles charging the lowest prices." Table 1 shows close to the opposite:

| Title | Price | Conversion |
|---|---|---|
| C | £7.99 | **2.4%** (highest) |
| A | £5.99 | 1.9% |
| D | £3.99 | 1.4% |
| B | £4.99 | **1.1%** (lowest) |

The most expensive title converts best. The proposed price of £4.99 matches the title that converts worst. Four titles cannot establish a price effect either way, because audience, local share and content probably matter more. Still, the data cannot support the stated conclusion, and Section 7 repeats it.

Take-up is also the wrong target. Revenue matters more. Title C earns about £75,000 a month in subscriptions, roughly twice Title A and four to five times Titles B and D. If the comparables point anywhere, it is towards a higher price.

### 2. The average conversion rate is wrong

The four rates average **1.7%**, not 2.0%: (1.9 + 1.1 + 2.4 + 1.4) / 4. The pooled rate is 1.77% (23,500 / 1,330,000). Correcting this changes the projection:

| Basis | Subscribers | Gross revenue at £4.99 |
|---|---|---|
| Paper (2.0%) | 8,400 | £503,000 |
| Simple average (1.7%) | ~7,140 | ~£428,000 |
| Pooled (1.77%) | ~7,420 | ~£444,000 |

### 3. Print cannibalisation is not addressed, and it could outweigh the gain

Section 2 reports that 30% of print subscribers would switch to a digital-only subscription under £6. The proposed £4.99 falls within that range. The paper never uses this finding.

Applied to the 11,200 print subscribers:
- About 3,360 switchers.
- Each loses £13.51 a month (£18.50 − £4.99).
- That is roughly **£545,000 a year** in lost revenue.

This exceeds the projected £358,000 net contribution even before the conversion correction. Some offsets apply:
- Stated intent usually overstates real behaviour.
- Survey respondents may not be representative.
- Fewer print copies save print and distribution costs.
- Some switchers may already be counted within the 8,400.

The paper needs to model this explicitly. It should also consider protective options: bundling digital access into print, pricing digital-only higher, or bundling at a discount for print subscribers. As it stands, the conclusion that the subscription "more than offset[s]" losses is unsupported.

### 4. Revenue is overstated in other ways

- **End-of-year count used for the full year.** 8,400 is the expected base at the end of year two, yet it is multiplied by twelve months as if present all year. The average base during the year will be lower.
- **Introductory offer ignored.** The £1-for-three-months offer cuts revenue from new subscribers by about £12 each. With 3–5% monthly churn, the base must be constantly replenished, so this cost recurs.
- **Churn not modelled.** Churn of 3–5% a month means roughly 250–420 lost subscribers a month at 8,400. Replacing them needs ongoing acquisition, which may not fit within the £60,000 marketing budget.

### 5. The comparables may not match the Courier's audience

Only about 60% of Courier MUU are in the circulation area. Out-of-area readers usually convert far less. Without knowing the comparables' local shares, applying their rates to all 420,000 MUU may overstate subscribers. A local-MUU basis (about 252,000) would be a useful sensitivity case.

## Minor issues

- **Advertising baseline.** The display loss is calculated on 2025 revenue of £1.1m, but revenue is falling about 12% a year. By year two the absolute loss will be smaller. The paper should say which year it is modelling.
- **Year-two timing.** "Year two" after a November 2026 launch runs to late 2028. The table should state that period clearly.
- **Fees.** Platform and payment fees of £85,000 are about 17% of revenue. Saying whether this is fixed or variable would show how costs scale if subscribers come in below projection.
- **Six-month review.** The comparables took about two years to stabilise, so a six-month review will see promotional-period data. The paper should say what that review can reasonably conclude.

## Arithmetic checks that hold

- Table 1 percentages are correct.
- 8,400 × £4.99 × 12 ≈ £503,000.
- £503,000 − £85,000 − £60,000 = £358,000.
- 5–8% of £1.1m = £55,000–£88,000.

## Recommendations

1. Correct the conversion rate and run low, central and high cases: 1.1%, 1.7% and 2.4%, on total and local MUU.
2. Rewrite Section 4 to match Table 1, and choose the price to maximise revenue rather than take-up. Test £5.99–£7.99.
3. Model print cannibalisation using the survey, with sensitivity for stated-versus-actual behaviour and print cost savings. Evaluate bundling options for print subscribers.
4. Build a month-by-month model with ramp-up, introductory pricing and churn, instead of applying an end-state count to a full year.
5. Restate the conclusion based on the corrected figures. On current evidence the case is not yet made, and it may reverse once cannibalisation is included.
